props.title: Eight hours on the deck
props.description: What a shift on a Bristol Bay gillnetter asks of a jacket, measured.
props.author: Ballard
paragraphs: We put two Salmon Bay Parkas on a 32-foot gillnetter for the July opener and logged what happened to them. Water on the deck is a mix of rain, spray, and hose. Hydrostatic head matters less than seam tape, because the seams are where the pressure concentrates when you kneel on a wet net.

Over 14 days, the shoulders took 3,200 hours of cumulative abrasion from net and line, measured by the crew's own count of hauls. The DWR on the shoulders was gone by day nine. The membrane held. No seam let go. Both hoods lost their wire brim shape by day twelve, which is why the current hood uses a stiffer wire.

Neither jacket needed repair after the season. One had a cuff Velcro replaced at the Fremont store because the crew member's watch had chewed it. That's the tradeoff of a hook-and-loop cuff: it's easy to adjust with gloves on and it wears out faster than a snap.
